content: Treatment for drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) involves the simultaneous use of multiple medications to address drug resistance and the slow growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This treatment typically includes an intensive phase with several drugs to rapidly reduce the bacterial load, followed by a continuation phase with fewer drugs to eliminate any remaining bacteria. Second-line TB drugs are primarily used for drug-resistant TB, although some first-line drugs may still be effective in certain cases. These second-line drugs are categorized into three groups (A, B, and C) to help design effective treatment regimens. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides specific treatment guidelines for different forms of drug resistance. In some cases, surgery, such as partial lung resection (lobectomy or wedge resection), may be considered as an adjunct to medical treatment to reduce the bacterial load and improve outcomes in patients with drug-resistant TB. Palliative care, as defined by WHO, focuses on preventing and alleviating the suffering of TB patients and their families. This care begins early in the disease course and is provided alongside life-prolonging therapies. It includes physical, psychological, emotional, and spiritual support, as well as planning and coordination of care. Palliative care also addresses stigma, discrimination, and access to social protection mechanisms, and it extends to bereavement support for families after a patient’s death. For rifampicin-susceptible but isoniazid-resistant TB, a six-month regimen of rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and levofloxacin is recommended. Injectable agents like streptomycin are not advised in these cases. Drug-resistant TB often arises from genetic mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, either due to inadequate treatment (secondary resistance) or transmission of resistant strains (primary resistance). For multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), a shorter all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline is recommended for eligible patients who have not been exposed to second-line TB drugs for more than one month and do not have fluoroquinolone resistance. Longer regimens for MDR/RR-TB should include all three Group A agents and at least one Group B agent, ensuring at least four effective drugs at the start of treatment. If Group A agents are limited, both Group B agents should be included, and Group C agents may be added if necessary. Kanamycin and capreomycin are not recommended, while levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid are strongly recommended for inclusion in longer regimens. Clofazimine, cycloserine, ethambutol, delamanid, and pyrazinamide may also be included under specific conditions. The total treatment duration for longer regimens is typically 18–20 months, with adjustments based on the patient’s response. For MDR-TB with additional fluoroquinolone resistance, a sixto nine-month regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) may be used under operational research conditions. Monitoring treatment response in MDR/RR-TB patients should include sputum culture in addition to smear microscopy, ideally performed monthly. Elective partial lung resection may be considered for MDR-TB patients as part of their treatment regimen. Ambulatory care is preferred over hospitalization for MDR-TB patients, and decentralized care models are recommended over centralized ones. TPT is recommended for people living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients (especially children), and other high-risk groups. Testing for LTBI can be done using a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). Preventive treatment options include daily isoniazid for six or nine months, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a four-month regimen of daily rifampicin. In high TB transmission settings, people living with HIV should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy, regardless of their antiretroviral therapy status, degree of immunosuppression, or history of TB treatment. Children under five years old who are household contacts of TB patients should receive TPT even if LTBI testing is unavailable. Preventive treatment may also be considered for selected high-risk household contacts of MDR-TB patients based on individual risk assessments. BCG vaccination is recommended for all infants as soon as possible after birth as part of routine immunization programs. Neonates born to mothers with confirmed pulmonary TB should receive TPT after active TB disease is excluded and should be regularly monitored. Children and young adolescents under 15 years old, particularly those living with HIV or in contact with TB patients, should be prioritized for TB prevention, early detection, and treatment. Shorter TPT regimens, such as three months of daily isoniazid and rifampicin (3HR) or weekly isoniazid and rifapentine (3HP), are preferred for children when appropriate.
